INTEREST OF AMICI CURIAE
The 	 American 	 Academy 	 of	 Pediatrics	 (“AAP”)
is an organization of 67,000 pediatricians, pediatric
medical subspecialists, and pediatric surgical specialists
committed to the optimal physical, mental, and social
health and well-being for all infants, children, adolescents,
and young adults. 1
The	 American	 College	 of	Physicians	 (“ACP”)	is	 the
largest medical specialty organization and the second
largest physician membership society in the United
States. ACP’s members include 161,000 internal medicine
physicians, related subspecialists, and medical students
who	 apply	 scientific	 knowledge,	 clinical	 expertise,	 and
compassion to the care of adults across the spectrum from
health to complex illness.
The National Medical Association is the collective
voice of African American physicians and the leading voice
for	parity	 and	justice	in	medicine	 and	the	elimination	 of
disparities in health.
The Connecticut State Medical Society is an
association representing over 4,000 physicians, residents,
and medical students in Connecticut. Its purposes include
the promotion of public health and safety in Connecticut.
1. This brief was not authored in whole or in part by counsel
for any party. No person or entity other than amici curiae , their
members, or their counsel made a monetary contribution to the
preparation or submission of this brief.

2
The Connecticut Chapter of AAP is an organization
of over 600 pediatricians in Connecticut, dedicated to
improving the health and safety of Connecticut’s children
and supporting those who provide their care.
The Illinois Chapter of AAP is an organization of over
2,000 pediatricians in Illinois, dedicated to improving the
health and well-being of infants, children, and adolescents
throughout Illinois.
Amici have a strong interest in these cases because
their members witness how dangerous and unusual the
military-style	 assault	 rifles	 like	 the	 AR-15	 are	 and	 the
enormous	 damage	 they	 inflict—the	 death,	 destruction,
chaos,	awful	injuries,	collateral	damage,	grief,	suffering,
and lifelong consequences. Amici respectfully submit
this brief to offer the unique perspective of healthcare
providers on the catastrophic effects of assault weapons
on the human body, their patients, their communities, and
their	 members.	 If	 victims	 of	 assault	 rifles	 survive	 long
enough to make it to the hospital, their lives are in the
hands of amici’s members. The emergencies and trauma
never end for them.
Amici’ s members understand the importance of
protecting our constitutional rights. They include many
individuals who grew up with and value the recreational
use	of	firearms	or	own	a	firearm	for	self-defense.
But amici’s members share the strong conviction,
informed by their healthcare work and research, that
assault rifles are fundamentally far more dangerous
than	 other	 firearms	 sold	to	 civilians.	 They	are	 the	type
of weapon that may be banned pursuant to current

3
constitutional doctrine. The Second and Fourteenth
Amendments do not prevent people, through their state
or local legislatures, from protecting their communities
by prohibiting AR-15s, and should not be interpreted to
impose any such restrictions. A ruling that prevents such
bans would have devastating consequences.
Amici respectfully submit that this is an appeal in
which this Court’s decision will directly affect whether
countless	people	live	or	die.	It	will	 be	a	legacy	decision—
not	 just	 for	our	 children	 and	 grandchildren	 but	 for	our
grandchildren’s grandchildren.
SUMMARY OF ARGUMENT
The question presented is whether the Second and
Fourteenth Amendments guarantee the right to possess
dangerous	 and	 unusual	 military-style	 assault	 rifles	 like
the	AR-15.	The	Court	should	answer	“no”	and	affirm 	the
decisions below.
Point	I	presents	 firsthand	 experiences	 of	just	 a	few
physicians who have treated victims of assault weapons,
including	both	patients	whose	deaths	and	severe	injuries
do not receive extensive coverage in the media and those
murdered	or	injured	in	some	of	the	most	infamous	 mass
shootings. 2
Point	II	explains	why	assault	rifles	are	extraordinarily
dangerous and unusual and a critical public health hazard.
2. The views of these physicians, expressed below, do not
necessarily 	reflect	the	views	of	any	entity	with	which	they	are	or
have	been	affiliated.

4
Point III shows the Constitution does not guarantee
the	right	to	possess	 AR-15s	or	other	assault	rifles.	 They
are	“like”	 the	M-16,	a	weapon	this	Court	has	said	can	be
banned. District of Columbia v. Heller, 554 U.S. 570, 627
(2008).	They	are	“dangerous	and	unusual	weapons.”	 Id.
ARGUMENT
I. PHYSICIANS HAVE FIRSTHAND KNOWLEDGE
OF THE ENORMOUS HARM CAUSED BY
ASSAULT RIFLES
A. Sandy Hook Elementary School and Dr.
William Begg
In approximately five minutes on December 14,
2012,	 a	shooter	used	an	AR-15	to	kill	 twenty	first-grade
children and six adults at Sandy Hook Elementary School
in	 Connecticut.	 The	 AR-15	 enabled	 the	 shooter	 to	 fire
about 154 shots, almost one bullet every two seconds he
was at the school.
Dr. Begg, the Endowed Chair of Emergency Medicine
at Danbury and New Milford Hospitals, Chairman of
the Board of Directors of the Newtown Health District,
Clinical Assistant Professor in the Department of Surgery
at the University of Vermont, and past recipient of the Dr.
Mark Quigley Award for Connecticut EMS Physician of
the Year, was the emergency physician on duty at Danbury
Hospital and the EMS Medical Director in contact with
the EMS personnel whose mission was to care for the
victims.

5
But not a single child struck by a bullet at Sandy
Hook survived. Most were not even sent to the hospital
because	 of	 the	 horrific	 injuries	 they	 suffered.	 Those
who did were dead on arrival. Each child was shot with
between three and eleven high-velocity bullets. Because
the bullets exploded in their little bodies, their organs
were obliterated, leaving nothing to resuscitate. For
example, Noah Pozner, age six, was shot once through
his	left	thumb,	once	in	his	face,	causing	“almost	complete
destruction”	of	his	jaw,	and	once	in	his	back.3	“The	bullet
that struck Noah’s back crossed through the center of his
chest,	filling	it	with	blood.	It	broke	apart	into	fragments.”4
Dr. Begg will never forget this. He believes gun
violence is a public health issue, and the people, through
their elected representatives, should be able to choose to
ban the AR-15 for civilians.
B. Dr. Selwyn Rogers’s and Dr. Edward Barksdale’s
Treatment of Assault Weapon Victims in
Chicago
Dr. Rogers, a trauma surgeon, and Dr. Barksdale,
a pediatric surgeon, at the University of Chicago’s
(“UChicago”)	 hospital,	 UChicago	 Medicine	 in	 the	South
Side of Chicago, treat victims of assault weapons on a

regular basis and have seen how dangerous and unusual

Dr. Rogers, who received his B.A. and M.D. from
Harvard, and was an Associate Professor of Surgery at
its Medical School, Chair of Surgery at Temple University
School of Medicine, and Professor of Surgery and Chief
Medical	 Officer	 at	University	 of	Texas	 Medical	 Branch,
is currently the James E. Bowman Jr. Professor in the
Biological Sciences at UChicago, Chief of Trauma and
Acute Care Surgery, Founding Director of UChicago’s
Level 1 trauma center, and Associate Editor of the New
England Journal of Medicine. Dr. Barksdale, who received
his B.S. from Yale and M.D. from Harvard, is a Professor
of Surgery and Pediatrics at UChicago, Chief Surgical
Officer	of	the	Chicagoland	Children’s	Health	A lliance,	and
a past recipient of Yale’s George Herbert Walker Bush ’43
Lifetime Leadership Award.
Both grew up in households with guns. Dr. Rogers’s
stepfather	 owned	 a	 rifle	 to	 hunt	 deer.	 Dr.	 Barksdale’s
mother kept a pistol at home to protect her family. But
both know from their experience treating victims of
assault	 rifles,	 and	 their	 research,	 that	 those	 weapons
are fundamentally different and unusually dangerous:
they	are	weapons	of	war	designed	to	kill	and	inflict	 mass
casualties, not to hunt or protect.
Dr. Rogers has witnessed the proliferation of assault
weapon violence from the operating table. Victims
generally have multiple wounds, unlike handgun shooting
victims, who generally have one or two bullet wounds.
There are also far more victims of each assault weapon
shooting. Because of the weapons’ light weight and lack

7
of recoil, a novice or even a ten-year-old can empty a
30-round magazine in seconds, spraying a dozen or more
people	 and	 killing	 or	 injuring	 even	 unintended	 targets.
That would have been impossible with a musket at the time
the Second Amendment was enacted because bystanders
back	then	could	have	scattered	 after	 the	first	 shot	while
the	shooter	reloaded.	The	damage	assault	weapons	inflict
is also extraordinarily different. They destroy flesh,
shatter	bones,	and	leave	victims	“unrecognizable.”
Dr. Barksdale has seen what assault weapons do to
children. Their power is so great that everything in the
path of their bullets is devastated. Blood vessels are clotted
off even when they are not directly hit. He previously saw
children struck by one or two bullets from a handgun. Now,
the children he sees who were shot by assault weapons
are struck by seven to ten bullets and have multiple
cavities similar to those military surgeons in Iraq and
Afghanistan have described. Many assault weapon victims
die. Those who survive can face permanent paralysis
and	other	lifelong	debilitating	 injuries	 requiring,	 among
other things, ventilators, tracheostomies, colostomies,
and wheelchairs.
Both Dr. Rogers and Dr. Barksdale have observed
that	 assault	 weapons	 do	 not	 just	 take	 lives—they	 take
whole lifetimes. They eliminate the possibility of a family
seeing a future for their child, and the ability of parents
and siblings to have their own lives when they must care
for	permanently	injured	children.	The	damage	they	inflict
extends far beyond the victims and their families to the
very fabric of their communities.

8
This violence persists in Chicago despite the assault
weapons bans because weapons are transported from
Indiana, Wisconsin, and other states that do not ban
them. But if Cook County’s and Illinois’s assault weapons
bans were struck down, access to assault weapons would
multiply	and	their	toll	would	significantly	increase.
C. Aurora Movie Theater and Dr. Barbara Blok
Dr. Blok, an Associate Professor of Emergency
Medicine and Associate Program Director for the Denver
Health Residency in Emergency Medicine, was on duty
on the night of July 20, 2012, when a shooter used an AR-
15	and	 other	 weapons	 to	 fire	 approximately	 seventy-six
bullets,	killing	twelve	people,	and	injuring	seventy	others
at a movie theater in Aurora, Colorado.
Dr. Blok treated twenty-three of the victims that
night. She saw the terrible destruction the AR-15 caused.
Patients suffered massive wounds, large tissue loss,
bowels hanging out of bellies, big wounds to the face
and scalp, and organs destroyed. Unlike a traditional
gunshot	wound	which	follows	the	trajectory	of	the	bullet,
the	injuries	from	the	AR-15	were	far	more	extensive	and
spread to surrounding tissue. Treating the victims had
a profound effect on everyone who provided care. Their
innocence was snatched away. Dr. Blok still feels grief and
sadness when she thinks about that night.
Dr. Blok grew up on a farm with family members
who used guns to hunt. She feels strongly that there is no
civilian	use	for	AR-15	assault	rifles.	They	are	unnecessary
killing machines that serve no hunting purpose. The

9
Court should not accept Petitioners’ request to remove
the people’s right to ban them.
D. San Bernardino and Dr. Kathleen Clem
Dr. Clem, a Professor at Dartmouth’s Geisel School
of Medicine, has worked as an emergency physician at
Level 1 trauma centers for more than twenty years, and
served	 as	 Chief	 Medical 	 Officer 	 and	 Vice	 President	 of
Florida Hospital in Orlando, Florida, Associate Professor
and Chief of the Division of Emergency Medicine in the
Duke University Department of Surgery, and Chairman
of the Level 1 Trauma Center Emergency Department at
the Loma Linda University Medical Center. A recipient
of the Duke University Distinguished Faculty Award and
the	A merican	College	of	Emergency	Physicians	(“ACEP”)
Hero of Emergency Medicine Award, she was on duty as
Director of the Loma Linda Emergency Department on
December 2, 2015, when two shooters armed with AR-
15-style	 military	 assault	 rifles	 and	 9mm	 semiautomatic
handguns entered the Inland Regional Center in San
Bernardino,	 California,	 fired	 approximately	 150	bullets,
killed 14 people, and wounded 21 others.
The	 most	seriously	 injured	 victims	 were	 brought	to
Dr. Clem’s hospital. She was in charge of ensuring that
the appropriate trauma teams were in place and oversaw
the victims’ treatment. She saw that the awful effects of
the	 assault	 rifles	 were	 not	 confined	 to	 the	 victims	 who
were shot. The entire community felt a fear and concern
for their safety that shootings with other weapons had
never caused.

10
Dr. Clem’s husband owns guns and uses them for
target shooting. Those guns are vastly different from the
AR-15. The AR-15 is not designed for sport or self-defense.
It is a weapon of war. It has no place in civilian hands.
E. Dr. Joanna Cohen’s Pediatric Emergency Care
Dr. Cohen, a pediatric emergency physician at Johns
Hopkins Children’s Center and Associate Professor of
Pediatrics at The Johns Hopkins School of Medicine, has
worked as a pediatric emergency physician at Children’s
National Hospital in Washington, D.C. and published
articles	on	firearm-related	injury	prevention.
In the last several years, Dr. Cohen has treated more
children who were shot than at any time in her career.
Patients	 have	 suffered	 devastating	 injuries	 including
to their spinal cords. They are now (and likely forever)
wheelchair bound, dealing with awful complications like
infections. They must be cared for by family members
whose lives are also forever changed by the additional
burden	and	psychological	injuries.
The	appalling	epidemic	of	firearm	violence	Dr.	Cohen
and her husband (also an emergency physician) witness
every day makes them perpetually anxious for their
children. They live in the city and are proud to be raising
“city	 kids”	 who	 go	 outside	 and	 are	 active.	 But	 firearm
violence	is	everywhere—including 	where	their	children
and many other children live and play. So now, when her
husband hears that an incoming patient is a shooting
victim,	 he	 asks	 “where?,”	 and	 then	 tries	 to	 determine
whether his children are there.

11
Dr. Cohen believes, based on her personal experience
treating	firearm	 violence	victims,	 that	assault	rifles	have
no place in civilian hands.
F.	 Dr. 	Michael	Hirsh’s	Treatment	of	Assault	Rifle
Victims
Dr. Hirsh, the son of Holocaust survivors who met
in a displaced persons camp, received his M.D. from
Harvard in 1979 and completed his residency in general
surgery at the Columbia Presbyterian Medical Center.
Now retired, he worked in pediatric surgery, trauma, and
critical care in Pittsburgh, before becoming a pediatric
trauma surgeon in Worcester, Massachusetts and serving
as Medical Director of its Department of Public Health.
When Dr. Hirsh’s mentor and friend was shot to
death outside their hospital after leaving to go home
to his ill pregnant wife, Dr. Hirsh resolved to dedicate
part of his life to addressing gun violence. A former
president	of	the	Injury	Free	Coalition	for	Children	and	the
Worcester District Medical Society, he worked to remove
assault weapons and other guns from his community
through buyback programs. The Worcester program has
collected	more	than	4,100	firearms	 and	given	out	at	least
1,200 trigger locks. Dr. Hirsh ran a similar program in
Allegheny County that collected more than 13,000 guns
in 29 years.
Dr. Hirsh has treated patients shot with an AK-47,
a	 Russian	 assault	 weapon	 that	 can	 fire	 multiple	 rounds
at high velocity, like the AR-15. When a person is shot,
it	 wreaks	 havoc	 not	 just	 in	 the	 bullet’s	 path,	 but	 in	 a
large surrounding radius. As the bullet spins like a drill,

12
nearby	tissue	implodes,	and	organs	turn	 to	“goo.”	When
a blood vessel is hit with a lower velocity bullet, there
is	 a	 possibility	 of	 repair.	 But	 the	 “blast	 effect”	 around
the	 trajectory	 of	 rapidly	 fired	 high-velocity	 bullets	 can
almost never be repaired. Because the bullets are not
easily stopped, they hit other structures and can knock
out swaths of tissue, amputate limbs, sever the spine,
and transect the body. The bleeding these weapons cause
is also far greater. Being shot is carnage in the truest
sense of the word. Dr. Hirsh believes they should not be
in civilian hands.
G. Tree of Life Synagogue and Dr. John Rozel
Dr. Rozel is a Professor of Psychiatry and Law at the
Center for Bioethics and Health Law at the University
of Pittsburgh. He teaches and consults on emergency
psychiatry and violence prevention internationally. Dr.
Rozel has published extensively on causes and prevention
of	firearm	violence.	He	has	responded	to	numerous	masscasualty events, including the October 27, 2018 mass
shooting at the Tree of Life synagogue in Pittsburgh
by	a	shooter	who	used	an	AR-15.	Dr.	Rozel	oversees	five
crisis programs across Western Pennsylvania, including
in high gun ownership and high gun crime communities.
His efforts to develop programs to prevent serious acts
of violence have earned him recognition from numerous
national and international organizations.
Dr. Rozel’s research and experience refute the
assertion	 that	 military-style	 assault	 rifles	 like	 the	 AR-
15 do not threaten public safety. Their wide availability
in states where they are legal can create dangerous
situations. In his home state of Pennsylvania, they can be

13
transferred quickly and legally between private parties
without a background check and without any oversight by
authorities	charged	with	keeping	dangerous	firearms	out
of the hands of unlawful possessors. The massive tissue

C. The Counting Exercise Proposed by Petitioners
Is Untenable
Petitioners’ attempt to force states and local
authorities	 to	 permit 	 assault	 rifles	 through	 a	 counting
exercise	based	on	“common	use”	today	is	not	supported	by
this Court’s decisions. Neither Heller nor Bruen	“posit[ed]
that a weapon’s common use is conclusive evidence that it
cannot	be	banned;”	“weapons	that	are	not in common use
can safely be said to be outside  the ambit of the Second
Amendment. But the logic does not work in reverse. Just
because a weapon happens to be in common use does not
nineteen 	 individuals	 armed	 with 	 a	 Revolutionary-era	 flintlock
rifle.”	And	since	they	did	not	exist	 when	the	Second	Amendment
was	 enacted,	 they	 cannot	 infringe	 the	 right	 “as	 originally
understood.”

37
guarantee that it falls within the scope of the right to keep
and	bear	arms.”	 Bianchi, 111 F .4th at 459-61.
Nor can a weapon’s dangerousness be dismissed
as	 constitutionally	 irrelevant.	 While	 all	 firearms	 are
“dangerous”	 to	 some	 degree,	 it	 does	 not	 follow	 that
courts may disregard differences in the magnitude of
that danger when determining whether a weapon is the
“type	 of	weapon”	protected	 by	the	Second	Amendment.
This Court should not be blind to the vast differences
between the handguns at issue in Heller and the assault
rifles	at	issue	here .
Petitioners	 appear	 to	 acknowledge	 that	 “unusually
dangerous”	weapons	fall	outside	the	Second	A mendment’s
protection.	 Yet	 they	 define	 “unusually	 dangerous”	 by
reference	to	purported	“common	use,”	making	the	inquiry
entirely	circular.	(Pet.	Br.	25	(“[B]y	definition,	an	arm	in
common	 use	 cannot	 be	 unusually 	 dangerous.”)).	 Under
this reasoning, no weapon, however destructive, could
ever	be	deemed	“unusually 	dangerous”	so	long	as	it	is	in
“common	use.”
Petitioners’ attempts to minimize the danger of
AR-15s are also unavailing. They note that some states
prohibit .223 caliber rifles for hunting large game
“because	 their	 rounds	lack	sufficient	 power,”	and	assert
that	assault	rifles	are	“not	inherently	more	dangerous	than
other	comparable	firearms”	because	they	“do	not	operate
differently	than	other	semiautomatics.”	(Pet.	Br.	9,	49).	But
the AR-15 was engineered to maximize human casualties
in combat, not to take large game. See Bianchi, 111 F.4th
at 451, 454-55, 463. And its extraordinary lethality derives
from	the	combination	of	its	design	features—not 	merely

38
its ammunition or its semiautomatic action. The fact that
an AR-15 and a Glock 19 handgun are both semiautomatic
does	not	make	them	equally	“dangerous.”	See Kolbe, 849
F .3d at 125.
Petitioners’	 proposed 	 “common 	 use” 	 test 	 is	 also
unworkable.	 They	 contend	 the	 “American	 people,”
not 	 “judges,”	 should	 decide	 whether	 a	 weapon 	 is
constitutionally protected.  (Pet. Br. 25). But under their
framework,	 judges	 would	 still	 determine	 whether	 a
weapon	qualifies 	as	in “common	use.”	And	because	there
are nearly unlimited metrics by which that determination
could	be	made,	Petitioners’	proposal	would	vest	in	judges,
not	 the	 “American	 people,”	 extraordinary	 discretion	 to
decide whether a weapon is protected.
Petitioners’ popularity test also would yield absurd
results. For example: States might be permitted to ban
“spears”	but	not	AR-15s (see Brief of United States at 17),
even	though	assault	rifles	are	vastly	more	destructive	than
any bladed weapon. And a ban on a weapon could become
unconstitutional	if	a	“sufficient”	number	of	people	illegally
acquire that weapon, even if a far greater number choose
not to do so.
Nor	have	the	“American	people”	made	any	collective
“decision”	that	AR-15s	are	not	“dangerous	and	unusual.”
(See Pet. Br. 25, 31). The legislatures of eleven states
and	 the	 District	 of	Columbia—representing	 118	million
people—have	 enacted	 assault	 weapons	bans.57 The bans

It is Petitioners, not Respondents, who seek to wrest
the	 “decision”	 on	 assault	 weapons	 from	 the	 people	 and
give it to this Court. But as Judge Wilkinson explained,
the	 Second	 Amendment	 “has	 not	disabled	 the	 ability	 of
representative democracy to respond to an urgent public
safety	 crisis.”	 Bianchi , 111 F .4th at 472. Nor does it
“require 	courts	to	turn	their	back	to	democratic	cries	…
at the very moment that lethal technologies are proceeding
at	an	accelerated	and	indeed	unprecedented	pace.”	Id. at
472-73.	 “Disenfranchising	 the	 American	 people	 on	 this
life	 and	 death	 subject	 …	 would	 deliver	 a	 body	 blow	 to
democracy as we have known it since the very founding
of	 this	 nation.”	 Kolbe, 849 F .3d at 150 (Wilkinson, J.,
concurring).
Affirming	 the	 decisions	 below	 would	 preserve	 the
status	quo.	Individuals	in	states	that	permit	assault	rifles
would	remain	 free	to	possess	 them.	Assault	 rifles	 would
be	 prohibited	 only	 in	 jurisdictions	 whose	 electorates
have democratically chosen to enact such prohibitions.
Conversely, if the Court holds that the Second Amendment
guarantees	 the	 right	 to	 possess	 assault	 rifles	 based	 on
a	 flawed	 interpretation	 or	 purported	 popularity	 test,	 it
would override the democratic choices of the people in the
states that have banned these weapons and the people in
the other states who would like to do so.
